## What Terraform is for

In Parts 4 and 5 you built the Lemonade Stand on AWS and Google Cloud by hand. You clicked through consoles and typed `aws` and `gcloud` commands. It worked, but three questions stay hard:

- **Can you do it again?** A new region, a staging copy, a rebuild after an accident means doing every step again, in the right order, without forgetting one.
- **What exactly is running?** After a month of small fixes, nobody remembers which settings were changed, or why.
- **What will this change break?** A click takes effect at once. There is no preview.

**Terraform** answers all three. You write down *what you want*, such as "one web server, one firewall rule, one menu bucket", in small text files. Terraform compares that wish list with what really exists, shows you the difference as a **plan**, and then makes reality match. The files live in Git, so every change can be reviewed, repeated and undone.

## The Lemonade Stand as code

```text
   you write                    Terraform                      real world
 ┌─────────────┐   plan    ┌──────────────────┐   apply   ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ main.tf     │ ───────▶  │ wish list  vs    │ ───────▶  │ Docker containers    │
 │ variables.tf│           │ state notebook   │           │ AWS EC2 + firewall   │
 │ outputs.tf  │ ◀──────── │ = list of changes│ ◀──────── │ Google Cloud Run     │
 └─────────────┘  outputs  └──────────────────┘  records  └──────────────────────┘
                                   │
                           terraform.tfstate (what Terraform built last time)
```

The same three steps repeat in every lesson: **write → plan → apply**.

## Run the lab with nothing but Docker

You do not need to install Terraform or create a cloud account. The official `hashicorp/terraform` image contains the whole tool. Define this helper once in your shell:

```bash
tf() {
  docker run --rm -it -e CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1 \
    -v "$PWD":/work -w /work \
    -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    hashicorp/terraform:1.17.2 "$@"
}
```

- `-v "$PWD":/work -w /work` shares the current folder with Terraform.
- `-v /var/run/docker.sock:...` lets Terraform start containers on your laptop. Only the Docker example needs it.
- `CHECKPOINT_DISABLE=1` turns off Terraform's "is there a newer version?" check, which can make commands hang inside a container.

Then `cd devops/terraform/examples/01-local` and run `tf init`, `tf plan` and `tf apply`. The [lab README](examples/README.md) lists every example.

| Folder | What it shows | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `examples/01-local/` | the first plan and apply: a menu file and a random stand name | Docker |
| `examples/02-docker/` | two real Lemonade web servers on `localhost:8088` and `:8089` | Docker |
| `examples/03-module/` | one module used twice | Docker |
| `examples/aws/` | an EC2 web server and a firewall rule on AWS | AWS account to apply; validate-only here |
| `examples/gcp/` | a public Cloud Run service | Google Cloud project to apply; validate-only here |

## Command cheat sheet

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `terraform init` | download providers and modules, set up the backend |
| `terraform fmt` | rewrite files in the standard style |
| `terraform validate` | check the files make sense, without touching anything real |
| `terraform plan` | show what would change |
| `terraform plan -out=tfplan` | save the plan so `apply` does exactly that |
| `terraform apply` | make the changes (asks for `yes`) |
| `terraform apply tfplan` | apply a saved plan, with no question asked |
| `terraform destroy` | delete everything this configuration created |
| `terraform output` | print the outputs, such as URLs |
| `terraform state list` | list everything Terraform is tracking |
| `terraform console` | try expressions and functions interactively |

## Clicking, Ansible or Terraform?

| Question | Clicking in a console | Ansible (Part 1) | Terraform |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main job | anything, once | configure software **inside** existing machines | create and delete the machines, networks and services **themselves** |
| Style | manual steps | a list of tasks, run in order (procedural, made idempotent by modules) | a description of the end result (declarative) |
| Preview before change | no | `--check --diff` (best effort) | `plan`, always |
| Remembers what it made | no | no (asks the hosts each time) | yes, in the **state** file |
| Deletes what you removed from the file | no | no, you write a task for it | yes |
| Typical Lemonade use | exploring | install nginx and the menu on `web1`, `web2` | create `web1`, `web2`, the firewall rule and the DNS name |

The tools work together. A common pattern, described by Yevgeniy Brikman in [*Terraform: Up & Running*](https://www.terraformupandrunning.com/), is to let Terraform build the servers and let Ansible, a container image or a startup script configure what runs on them.
